messages.author: 983257fd4b8064bd
messages.subject: MSOM with improbably high intercepts
parts:
Hello all,

I have a MSOM that gives improbably high estimates for the intercepts (0.999+ for all species). I wondered if it was something to do with my choice of priors, so I have tried a huge range of hyperpriors for the detectability and occupancy intercepts, from norm(0,0.01) to norm(0,1) and logistic(0,1). Nothing seems to make any difference. I have used the same model structure with the same set of predictors with other taxa using logistic(0,1) priors throughout, and the models run fine and produce realistic outputs.

The troublesome model has 89 species at 79 sites, with 2 - 4 visits per site. Structure is a standard MSOM, as per AHM1 chapter 11, but also includes a variance-covariance element to account for common species being more detectable (see attached). There are 16 occupancy slope parameters (10 linear, 6 interactions), and 2 detectability slope parameters. I run the model with 100k iterations, 50k adaptations and 50k burn-in. Rhats are ok, although n.effs are often small (~100 - 300). Detectability estimates are mostly very low, which I guess is then leading to the very high occupancy estimates.

Can anyone recommend a way to deal with this, please? Is there a combination of priors that will help? Or do I need to revisit the model structure? I would really prefer  not to change the structure, as I want to use the same for all taxa. But if I do have to think about that, what can I change that might help?

Many thanks,
Tom

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: MSOM with improbably high intercepts
parts:
Dear all,

so I played around with Tom's analysis of a static, multi-species occupancy model, which estimated occupancy near 1 for all species. Unfortunately, this is a report of non-progress. However, we wanted to share it in case somebody else has some hunch what could be the source of the problem.

At the start, I had to main hunches about what could be the source of the problems:
  • Tom's use of flattish priors for the occupancy and detection intercepts on the logit scale, which translate to the famous bath-tub shape on the probability scale, where most mass is near 0 or 1. These might have pushed occupancy towards 1.
  • Small sample sizes and few sites with observations, plus possibly small detection probs, which might lead to a positive bias in occupancy
Unfortunately, both proved to be wrong.

The data set has 89 species of moths surveyed in up to 4 occasions at 79 sites. The data are fairly "ecological" in the sense of being quite imbalanced: many sites have fewer than 4 surveys. Looking at the raw data did not show anything exceptional, and the observed proportion of occupied sites was reasonable. Here's a summary of that:

> summary(psiobs)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
0.01266 0.06329 0.10127 0.19414 0.25316 0.91139

The detection-nondetection matrix contains 17,000 non-missing entries, with 90% zeroes and 10% ones. I don't think this suggests extremely low detection probs.

Here are some of the things that I tried out:
  • Tom's original model had lots of covariates in occupancy and a couple in detection, plus an occupancy-detection correlation. I immediately discarded all that complexity and worked with an intercepts-only model without correlation. The problem of near-1 occupancy estimates persisted in this stripped-down model.
  • I then specified the priors for the mean hyperparameters for both occupancy and detection as U(0,1) on the probabilty scale, as in the following, but that did not help either.
  # Hyperpriors for occupancy
  # mu.lpsi ~ dnorm(0,0.01)   # Original prior on the logit intercept
  mu.lpsi <- logit(mean.psi)  # New prior on the probability-scale intercept
  mean.psi ~ dunif(0, 1)      
  • Then I tried to implement the scale prior of Link (Ecology, 2013), which didn't work at all. (Although, to be honest, I am a little sceptic about whether I did that right.)
  • Next, I stripped down the model to one with fixed species-level effects, by removing the hierarchical community structure. This worked well and yielded estimates that appeared to make much more sense for this data set. Here is a summary of the posterior means of the 89 estimates of psi and of p in this model, which is equivalent to fitting the simplest, static, single-species occupancy model to the data from each species one at a time:

  • > summary(out0$mean$psi)
       Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
     0.1730  0.3460  0.5214  0.5377  0.6974  0.9593

  • > summary(out0$mean$p)
       Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
    0.08497 0.11757 0.15180 0.18456 0.21682 0.71742

  • As a final straw, I went back to the hierarchical version of the model and tried to constrain the priors for the hyperparameters ever so slightly away from their boundaries, but this didn't materially change anythying:

  •   # Hyperpriors for hyperparams
      mu.lpsi <- logit(mu.psi)
      mu.psi ~ dunif(0.01, 0.99)
      tau.lpsi <- pow(sig.lpsi, -2)
      sig.lpsi ~ dunif(0.01, 5) # Also here constrain away from the bound

I find this really puzzling and have never seen anything like it when fitting community occupancy models. Perhaps somebody else has any ideas ? It might also be worth trying to fit the model using the apparently superior posterior-exploration abilities of HMC in software NIMBLE or Stan ?

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: MSOM with improbably high intercepts
parts:
Dear all,

here's an interesting idea about the problem in Tom's model from Rahel Sollmann. She writes:

"one thing comes to mind (although I kind of doubt that that's the reason - see below): looking at the summary of species-specific estimates of p in the non-hierarchical suite of single-species models, the distribution of p-values looks pretty non-normal: the mean and median are <0.2 but the max is >0.7 (the skew persists on the logit scale). Maybe the normal hyperprior is to blame and a different distribution should be used? Have you looked at a histogram of detection probabilities - maybe their distribution is multi-modal? Results for psi are a lot more evenly spread between 0 and 1, that's why I am suspecting p to be the problem. 

On the other hand, based on my own experiments with the Dirichlet process as a hyper-distribution (which allows for multiple modes), the regular Normal hyperdistirbution always worked just as well. That's why I don't think this is likely to be the issue. But easy to look at by plotting a histogram of p; and also easy to test by putting hierarchical structure on psi but keeping a fixed species effect on p. If that works ok, at least you'd know the issue is with the detection component of the model."

This is a question about whether the usual Gaussian assumptions about random effects are adequate or not (and there is some literature out there, both in the context of classical mixed models and also in the context of community occupancy models; see here: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/eap.2249).

However, here are 4 histograms of both parameters in Tom's analysis, on the probability and on the logit scale. In the two latter, I superimposed a normal density with mean and sd estimated from the species-level parameter estimates. I think these Gaussian approximations don't look fantastic, but I have definitely seen worse. So probably that's not the cause of the problem.
Best regards  --- Marc

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: Matthijs Hollanders <matthijs....@gmail.com>
Date: Fri, Oct 14, 2022 at 7:31 AM
Subject: Re: MSOM with improbably high intercepts

To: Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>


Hi all,

I also had a go at this in nimble because I was fascinated. TL;DR, I got nowhere. 

Like Marc I got rid of all complexity and fitted hierarchical and fixed effect priors on species-level psi and p. Attached are the plots for the estimates of each. I used centered and non-centered parameterization of the hierarchical priors and also tried Student-t priors to see if that made a difference, which it didn't. I used weakly informative dlogis(0, 1) and dexp(1) priors for the population mean and SD of the hierarchical intercepts, and dlogis(0, 1) for the fixed effect intercepts on the logit scale.

I would suggest going to the nimble-users forum and asking them. I don't think there's many issues that have gone unresolved over there. Feel free to use my code to share, which is attached in a Quarto doc.

Cheers,

Matt

      sig.lpsi ~ dunif(0.01, 5) # Also here constrain away from the bound

I find this really puzzling and have never seen anything like it when fitting community occupancy models. Perhaps somebody else has any ideas ? It might also be worth trying to fit the model using the apparently superior posterior-exploration abilities of HMC in software NIMBLE or Stan ?

Best regards  --- Marc

Betreff: MSOM with improbably high intercepts

 

Hello all,

 

I have a MSOM that gives improbably high estimates for the intercepts (0.999+ for all species). I wondered if it was something to do with my choice of priors, so I have tried a huge range of hyperpriors for the detectability and occupancy intercepts, from norm(0,0.01) to norm(0,1) and logistic(0,1). Nothing seems to make any difference. I have used the same model structure with the same set of predictors with other taxa using logistic(0,1) priors throughout, and the models run fine and produce realistic outputs.

 

The troublesome model has 89 species at 79 sites, with 2 - 4 visits per site. Structure is a standard MSOM, as per AHM1 chapter 11, but also includes a variance-covariance element to account for common species being more detectable (see attached). There are 16 occupancy slope parameters (10 linear, 6 interactions), and 2 detectability slope parameters. I run the model with 100k iterations, 50k adaptations and 50k burn-in. Rhats are ok, although n.effs are often small (~100 - 300). Detectability estimates are mostly very low, which I guess is then leading to the very high occupancy estimates.

 

Can anyone recommend a way to deal with this, please? Is there a combination of priors that will help? Or do I need to revisit the model structure? I would really prefer  not to change the structure, as I want to use the same for all taxa. But if I do have to think about that, what can I change that might help?

 

Many thanks,

Tom

messages.subject: WG: MSOM with improbably high intercepts
parts:
Dear all,

 

a quick follow-up on Tom’s model, where adding hierarchical (community) structure to a multi-species-occupancy model lets the species-specific parameter estimates jump to the boundaries (1 for occupancy, 0 for detection).

 

Matthijs Hollanders gave it a try in Nimble. He did this: “I got rid of all complexity and fitted hierarchical and fixed effect priors on species-level psi and p. Attached are the plots for the estimates of each. I used centered and non-centered parameterization of the hierarchical priors and also tried Student-t priors to see if that made a difference, which it didn't. I used weakly informative dlogis(0, 1) and dexp(1) priors for the population mean and SD of the hierarchical intercepts, and dlogis(0, 1) for the fixed effect intercepts on the logit scale.”

 

This didn’t help either. So the mystery is still unsolved …

 

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.author: 42d256fc3b96b0e5
messages.subject: Re: MSOM with improbably high intercepts
parts:
Hello,

Just a stab in the dark here. But is it the case that a relatively small proportion of the more common species a) occur at almost all of the sites (very high occupancy), and as a result of this, b) somehow contribute a large proportion of the presence data, and have very tight estimates of high occupancy probabilities?

If that were the case you might expect intercepts for other species with more uncertainty in intercepts,, and less data to pool towards intercepts for the more highly represented common species (with high occupancy).

It might be interesting to drop some of the more ubiquitous species and see how the model behaves.

Very happy to be told why I'm wrong on this!

Cheers,
Tadhg
